entries.content:
Will Yin

CEO, Visko

Ivan Nardini

Developer Relations Engineer, Google Cloud

Editor's note: Generative AI startups are moving rapidly beyond static clip generation to build interactive, real-time worlds. In this technical deep dive, we explore how AI startup Visko collaborated with Google Cloud TPU engineers to deploy Orbis — its continuously streaming Live World Model—on Cloud TPUs, going from initial kickoff to production handover in just 30 days.

What makes a live video world model so challenging to serve in production? The bottleneck isn't average throughput — it's beating a relentless real-time clock. Unlike offline video generators where a user submits a prompt and waits in a queue, a live world model streams continuously. Every new chunk of video and synchronized audio must finish rendering before the viewer finishes watching the previous one, or the world freezes.

Today, we're excited to share how Visko, an AI startup pioneering interactive world models, teamed up with Google Cloud to solve this exact challenge. Working side by side, Visko and Google Cloud engineers deployed Visko's end-to-end live inference pipeline — combining video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio—onto a single Cloud TPU slice. Together, the teams brought end-to-end generation down, rendering at 1.07x playback speed.

Here is an inside look at how we engineered the pipeline to hit that milestone in a single month, the architectural optimizations that moved the needle, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI on Google Cloud.

Redefining interactive media with Live World Models

While most generative video platforms focus on rendering fixed, pre-baked clips, Visko is building what it calls Live Models: video world models that generate continuously and respond on the fly.

Visko's flagship model, Orbis, streams live video starting from a single text or image prompt. As the stream plays, viewers can enter new steering prompts in real time, dynamically evolving the scene without restarting or breaking continuity. For instance, in one test session, the livestream opens on a cat napping beside a crackling fireplace; when the viewer steers the scene to introduce a bowl of food, the bowl materializes seamlessly, and the cat stretches, stands up, and meows.

Since launching its public demo on September 1, 2026, Orbis has unlocked new possibilities across interactive entertainment, live commerce, AI companions, immersive education, and robotics simulation. To scale these interactive sessions reliably, Visko partnered with Google Cloud TPU engineers in August 2026 to port the Orbis live pipeline to Google's Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). Within 30 days, the full multimodal pipeline was running in real time on TPUs.

Visko’s ambition is to power a new generation of interactive worlds that people can step into and shape in real time. Streaming continuous video and audio under a strict clock is a fundamentally different system challenge than offline clip generation. Working side by side with Google Cloud's TPU engineers, we brought the full Orbis pipeline to TPUs in just 30 days — giving us the low-latency compute and memory bandwidth required to bring Live Models to creators and developers at scale.

"Visko is bringing an exciting new class of real-time, steerable workloads to the Cloud TPU ecosystem. By co-engineering their live multimodal pipeline on a singleTPU slice using JAX, torchax, and custom Pallas kernels, we proved how quickly a lean startup team can go from PyTorch prototype to render at 1.07x playback speed on Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer."

– Dave Elliott, Head of Developer Advocacy for AI, Google Cloud 

Live video is a hard-deadline problem

When you serve an offline clip generator, latency is forgiving — the user waits once while the backend processes frames. A live world model has no waiting room.

Every single chunk must be denoised, decoded from latents, upscaled to 1664x936 (at 18 fps), and paired with generated audio faster than realtime playback speed, for as long as the session runs.

Two structural constraints make live world models far more demanding than standard batch inference:

  • Batch size of one: Each live stream represents an individual viewer's interactive session. You cannot mask latency by grouping dozens of concurrent requests into a massive batch — the standard playbook for keeping AI accelerators saturated.

  • Strict sequential dependency: Every chunk depends directly on the one before it. Because the video model maintains a rolling memory of recent video latents so that chunk N+1 smoothly continues the action from chunk N, you cannot pre-render chunks out of order or parallelize across future timestamps.

For startup infrastructure engineers coming from LLM serving, it helps to think of live world modeling not as a tokens-per-second throughput benchmark, but as an unforgiving per-step latency SLO.

Architecting the multimodal pipeline on a single TPU slice

To keep infrastructure lean and cost-effective as Visko scales, the team designed the live pipeline to chain three distinct generative models on a single Cloud TPU slice running in BF16 precision.

When a viewer submits an initial prompt or a live steering update, all three generative models — the core video diffusion model, the super-resolution upscaler, and the audio generator — share the same chips, taking turns on the hardware for each chunk.

Figure 1: Visko's end-to-end Orbis live pipeline chains video diffusion, latent decoding, super-resolution upscaling, and pure-JAX audio generation sequentially on a single Cloud TPU slice, completing each chunk faster than the playback speed.

To combine rapid startup iteration with bare-metal accelerator speed, the software stack is built on three open-source pillars:

  • JAX: Google's high-performance Python array library for accelerators, compiled into optimized machine code by the XLA compiler.

  • torchax: An interoperability layer that runs PyTorch models directly on Cloud TPUs via JAX, enabling startup teams to bring existing PyTorch components over without an upfront, ground-up rewrite.

  • Pallas: The custom kernel programming language for TPUs in JAX — the TPU counterpart to writing custom Triton or CUDA kernels on GPUs.

Real-time performance breakdown: Hitting the clock

By profiling and optimizing each stage on a single slice in BF16, the engineering team achieved a total per-chunk latency of under the target while — maintaining roughly 7% headroom to absorb variance during live streaming:

Figure 2: Chart of per-chunk latency budget on one TPU slice.

Because video denoising accounts for nearly two-thirds of the total compute budget, that stage became the primary focus of our kernel and parallelism optimizations.

Inside the stack: Three optimizations that unlocked real-time streaming

1. Ulysses context parallelism across all TPU chips

A video chunk expands into a massive sequence of spatiotemporal tokens inside the video transformer. To distribute that workload across the TPU chips at batch size 1, the team implemented Ulysses context parallelism.

Instead of splitting model weights, Ulysses splits the token sequence across chips. Immediately before the attention layer, a high-speed all-to-all interconnect exchange regroups the tensors so that each chip holds the entire video sequence, but only for one-quarter of the attention heads. After each chip computes attention over the full sequence for its assigned heads, a second all-to-all exchange restores the sequence-split layout for the feed-forward layers.

Figure 3: Ulysses context parallelism across TPU chips at batch size 1. High-speed all-to-all Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) exchanges transition tensors between a sequence-split layout for feed-forward layers and a head-split layout for Pallas splash attention.

2. Custom Pallas splash attention from MaxDiffusion

To accelerate the attention computation itself, the team integrated a custom Pallas splash attention kernel from MaxDiffusion, Google Cloud's open-source reference library for diffusion models on Cloud TPU.

Splash attention brings FlashAttention-style tiling to TPU architecture: rather than materializing the full quadratic attention matrix in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), it computes attention in compact tiles that remain inside ultra-fast on-chip VMEM. Startup teams can drop the exact kernel used in this port straight into their own pipelines via custom_splash_attention.py.

3. A 5.8x audio speedup by moving from torchax to pure JAX

We first brought all three Orbis models onto Cloud TPU with *torchax*, which runs PyTorch code on TPU through JAX and XLA without a rewrite. For the video and upscaling models, `torchax` paired with Pallas attention kernels met our latency target directly, and both stay in `torchax` in the final pipeline.

Only the audio model needed a rewrite. Moving the audio stage from `torchax` to *native JAX* made it *5.8x faster* and brought the full pipeline under the playback deadline.

Startup Builder Tip: Port strategically.

The takeaway isn't "skip torchax" — it's to use it as a fast bring-up bridge. torchax got our PyTorch models running on TPU in days rather than weeks, giving us the end-to-end telemetry needed to pinpoint true bottlenecks. Measure the full pipeline first, and invest engineering cycles rewriting only the components that dominate your latency budget.

Field notes for AI builders: Cloud TPU lessons

Takeaways from tuning live multimodal inference on Cloud TPU:

- *Ulysses context parallelism for single stream video:* At batch size 1, splitting the token sequence across chips with `all-to-all` interconnect exchanges was faster than both tensor parallelism and ring attention.

- *Native BF16 for continuous streams:* FP8 quantization cuts memory bandwidth pressure, but small quantization errors build up across chunks in a continuous stream. Native BF16 kept visual quality intact within the latency budget.

- *Selective JAX ports:* `torchax` kept the video and upscaling models in PyTorch, so the team only rewrote the audio bottleneck in native JAX.

- *XLA compilation caching:* The first boot spends a few minutes compiling XLA graphs. Caching compiled artifacts brings worker restarts under a minute.

Building real-time generative models on Cloud TPU? Start here

If your startup is pushing the boundaries of live video, world models, or ultra-low-latency multimodal inference, you can build with the same toolkit that powered Visko's port:

  • Accelerate diffusion attention out of the box: Grab the open-source splash attention kernel used in this collaboration from MaxDiffusion, and explore the Pallas documentation to write custom TPU kernels.

  • Migrate PyTorch fast, then optimize selectively: Bring your existing PyTorch models onto TPU quickly with torchax, pinpoint bottlenecks with the Cloud TPU Profiler, and port latency-critical stages to native JAX.

  • Spin up TPUs on demand: Use TPU Flex-start VMs to provision TPU capacity for short development and benchmarking runs without a long-term reservation.

  • Scale with Google for Startups: Early-stage AI startups looking for cloud credits, technical mentorship, and access to Google Cloud's AI Hypercomputer stack can apply to the Google for Startups Cloud Program.

Special thanks to the Visko.ai team for the close technical partnership, and to the Google Cloud TPU engineers who lead the project including: Yixin Shi, James Huang, and Elisa Tsai.

entries.title: Bringing the borderless Lakehouse into the agentic era with innovations for Gemini
entries.summary: As enterprises shift their AI usage from experimental chatbots to autonomous agents, teams are hitting a critical bottleneck: accessing and reasoning over data scattered across multiple clouds, SaaS platforms, and on-premises systems. To turn AI agents into true systems of action, organizations need a foundation that can handle petabyte-scale reasoning without the security risks of data movement.
entries.content:
Gaurav Saxena

Director, Product Management

Ahmet Altay

Director, Engineering

As enterprises shift their AI usage from experimental chatbots to autonomous agents, teams are hitting a critical bottleneck: accessing and reasoning over data scattered across multiple clouds, SaaS platforms, and on-premises systems. To turn AI agents into true systems of action, organizations need a foundation that can handle petabyte-scale reasoning without the security risks of data movement. Last week at our Gemini at Work event, we announced how Gemini can help you transform business workflows. To help power your agents with your enterprise data, we will dive deeper into the new Gemini integration with borderless Lakehouse to help you build, secure, and scale agents that work across your data estate.

Access data that lives outside of Google Cloud through Gemini

The ultimate value of the borderless Lakehouse is realized through the agents you build to transform your organization, with Gemini as the front door. With the new Gemini integration, data that’s either preconfigured or stored in your borderless Lakehouse is now directly integrated into Gemini. Currently in preview, this means you can set up access to new data sources, such as Databricks Unity Catalog or Snowflake Horizon, through Lakehouse catalog federation directly from Gemini.

Now your business users can use natural language to query records that live across clouds while your AI agents can ground their reasoning and generate code from the same data — all without moving it. By directly contextualizing AI agents across your borderless Lakehouse, you can help accelerate your organization’s AI adoption while simplifying access to critical information.

Gemini agents invoked by business users can access data that lives in BigQuery and Databricks Unity Catalog to provide comprehensive reporting and get insights using natural language.

Borderless Lakehouse advancements

In addition to this new, native integration with Gemini, we’re sharing that several features we introduced earlier this year to power your data foundation with the borderless Lakehouse are now generally available, including:

  • Support for Cross-Cloud Interconnect and cross-cloud caching for AWS and Azure

  • BigQuery support for Apache Iceberg V3 specifications

  • Read-write interoperability on Apache Iceberg tables for both BigQuery and Managed Service for Apache Spark

  • Support for AlloyDB lakehouse federation

  • Bi-directional caching with AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, and Snowflake Horizon Catalog using Lakehouse runtime federation

  • Integration with Knowledge Catalog

  • Zero-copy data integration with Salesforce, SAP and Workday, and now, Confluent Tableflow

  • Synchronization of Databricks Delta Lake assets through the Lakehouse console using Dataflow

Let’s explore.

Performance and reasoning at petabyte scale

While agent context windows are typically limited to ingesting hundreds of kilobytes at a time, enterprise workflows sometimes join petabytes of data across clouds. An agent-native data platform that needs to combine data across sources, like product and customer data, to your CRM cloud and warehouse telemetry needs to be able to process data at scale. When you do this over MCP, you are limited to megabyte scale because of context windows and payload size. By integrating at every layer of the data and AI stack, the borderless Lakehouse provides enterprise-grade scalability, enabling agents to reason over petabytes of data with similar performance to it being stored locally.

At the networking layer, Cross-Cloud Interconnect and cross-cloud caching provide high-throughput, low-latency paths to AWS and Azure, eliminating variable egress fees. When an agent joins Iceberg tables in Amazon Azure Data Lake Storage with data in BigQuery, every uncached byte it scans crosses a cloud boundary, so the network sets the pace. Cross-Cloud Interconnect gives the Lakehouse a dedicated, private connection between Google Cloud and AWS or Azure, at 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps per connection. Lakehouse queries travel over that connection rather than the public internet, so latency stays low and predictable. Cross-cloud caching serves repeat reads from inside Google Cloud, so agents can query data in other clouds without migrating it.

The borderless Lakehouse includes several key optimizations to integrate Iceberg metadata within the query engine. BigQuery now supports Apache Iceberg V3 specifications, including binary deletion vectors and sort orders. These features allow the engine to handle row-level updates and deletes more efficiently by eliminating the need to rewrite entire data files. We also upgraded BigQuery’s execution engine with a new FlatBuffers-based Parquet reader and parallelized I/O to help reduce CPU overhead and serialization bottlenecks and narrow the performance gap between open formats and native storage.

This builds upon recent performance innovations to the query engine designed to support agent workloads, which often come in herds and need to process small queries quickly and cost effectively. With BigQuery fluid scaling and history based optimizations, you can run scalable and efficient agent workloads while maintaining openness with Apache Iceberg. 

Meanwhile, read-write interoperability on Apache Iceberg tables for both BigQuery and Managed Service for Apache Spark makes it easy for all of your data teams to work off the same Iceberg tables in Google Cloud Storage. This vertically optimized stack helps make your agents faster and more cost-effective, leveraging the power of BigQuery and Lightning Engine to activate data without moving it. To expand the analytical depth of the lakehouse, graph support for Iceberg in BigQuery lets you analyze relationship networks, such as supply chains, directly on open table datasets.

Then, for operational data, AlloyDB lakehouse federation lets you query live database records and historical warehouse data together from a single connection without copying any information. This simplifies your system and lowers costs while giving agents instant access to both real-time updates and deep background history with the borderless Lakehouse.

Comprehensive context and data access for your agents

An AI agent is only as smart as the context it can access. To help prevent hallucinations and improve accuracy at the metadata layer, the borderless Lakehouse unifies your enterprise data using the Lakehouse runtime catalog. Based on the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog, it provides bi-directional catalog federation with AWS Glue, Databricks Unity Catalog, and Snowflake Horizon Catalog. The Lakehouse runtime catalog also includes a new standard Hive Metastore-compatible endpoint, allowing engines like Apache Spark, Trino, and Presto to discover metadata without architectural changes. 

The borderless Lakehouse also integrates directly with Knowledge Catalog, which automatically indexes your distributed data assets, to provide the precise business metadata and semantic definitions agents need to reason over your entire enterprise corpus — including unstructured data in Cloud Storage. This gives agents just enough context to be accurate while controlling token costs, helping you develop an intelligent and sustainable agentic strategy. 

The borderless Lakehouse provides zero-copy data integration with your SaaS applications like Salesforce, SAP and Workday and integrates with a larger partner ecosystem, capturing enterprise data in Knowledge Catalog and acting as a single context engine for your agents. Today, we’re expanding the partner ecosystem with new integrations for Confluent Tableflow, now generally available, which syncs to Lakehouse runtime catalog so the Iceberg tables it produces show up directly in BigQuery, with no copying and no extra ETL.

Finally, organizations with Databricks-centric repositories can now easily import, transform and synchronize their Delta Lake assets into Lakehouse through the Lakehouse console using Dataflow.

Modernize with ease

Customer use of Apache Iceberg has more than tripled since the beginning of 2025, and enterprises building with Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse are seeing significant impact from it:

  • Etsy unified three petabytes with borderless Lakehouse, joining data in place to accelerate pipeline queries by 60%. 

  • Commerzbank transforms raw distributed data into governed, agent-ready access.

  • Hightouch integrates directly with borderless Lakehouse so teams can power their marketing directly on an open Iceberg lakehouse and activate that data across the Google Cloud ecosystem.

  • Roundel modernized its Target Product Ads technology stack from the ground up with borderless Lakehouse, completely rebuilding its data ingestion, processing, and measurement pipelines. 

If you are ready to get started with the transition to borderless Lakehouse for your organization, it doesn’t need to be difficult. For organizations currently using legacy Dataproc Metastore, we now offer an automated, zero-downtime migration path to the serverless Lakehouse runtime catalog. This preserves your existing schemas and lineage while unlocking the AI-ready features of the borderless Lakehouse, so you can stop managing infrastructure and start activating agents.

Get started today with the Build a borderless Lakehouse codelab or visit our website to learn more.

entries.content:
Sagar Randive

Product Manager

Aniruddh Chaturvedi

Engineering Manager

The open-source Temporal execution platform is rapidly becoming a foundational layer of modern software infrastructure — especially for orchestration in distributed systems and AI agent workloads. However, deploying and scaling workers in Temporal comes with unique challenges. Workers poll for tasks instead of serving requests, so request-driven serverless platforms can be an awkward fit. This often results in running worker fleets on Kubernetes or VMs, which you have to manage and pay for continuously. You build a metrics pipeline and tune autoscaling triggers, and scaling still trails bursts because of metrics lag. Every deployment means juggling upgrades and versions, and you pay for that compute whether or not there's work in the queue.

We built Cloud Run worker pools for exactly this kind of pull-based work: Your instances connect to a queue or stream, take the next item, and process it. Starting today, Temporal Cloud, which is the fully managed version of Temporal’s open-source platform, can scale them for you. Currently in preview, Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run let you deploy your workers as a worker pool, and Temporal sizes the pool to match the work on your task queues. When there's no work, it can scale the pool to zero. There's no cluster or autoscaler to run, and your worker code stays the same.

How Cloud Run worker pools fit with Temporal

A worker pool is Cloud Run's resource for continuous background work. It has no public endpoint, and each instance is allocated CPU for its whole lifetime, which matches how a Temporal worker runs. Temporal manages your Cloud Run worker pools as follows:

  • Your Temporal workers run as Cloud Run worker pool instances in your project and poll Temporal Cloud for tasks.

  • Temporal Cloud tracks your task queues and sets the worker pool's instance count through the Cloud Run Admin API, using the IAM permissions you grant. Temporal never opens a connection to your instances, so you don't need to open ports or add firewall rules for it.

  • You run each build version as its own Cloud Run worker pool. An older build's worker pool can sit at zero instances until a workflow that started on it needs it again.

Your Temporal workers run in your project, under your service account, and on your network. Temporal decides how many of them run.

What you can build with Temporal Serverless Workers

The combination of Cloud Run worker pools with Temporal Serverless Workers opens up a variety of interesting use cases:

Autoscaled agentic workers: AI agents run multi-step chains of LLM reasoning and tool calls. Temporal's durable execution and Cloud Run worker pools work together here. Temporal workers spin up instantly to handle bursts of LLM steps, embeddings or API calls, then scale to zero when the queue empties. Workers get keyless access to Google Cloud AI APIs. You can also attach a GPU for inference, and the workers attached to the GPUs will still scale to zero. Temporal runs each model and tool call as a durable activity; if a worker disappears mid-step, the activity retries on another worker and the workflow continues.

Long-running Workflows: Temporal Workflows can run indefinitely, allowing for building applications that track the state of real-world resources over long periods of time. This pattern is typically known as the “Entity Pattern,” because the Workflow represents the state of some entity. However, these long-running Workflows don’t usually have consistent compute requirements: Some individual steps are short, some are long, and other times, the Workflow is sleeping, waiting for external input, such as from a human or another system. Cloud Run worker pools provide flexible compute to support this pattern: Individual steps can run for as long as is required, and Temporal will automatically scale down the worker pool when there is no work to be done. 

Bursty batch work: Worker pools bill only while instances run, so a worker pool that sits idle between batch runs costs nothing while it's at zero instances. For jobs like billing runs or media transcoding, Temporal scales the pool out as batches arrive and back in once the queue drains. Your maximum instance count caps how many instances you pay for. Tasks beyond that capacity wait in the queue rather than being dropped.

Why Cloud Run worker pools for Temporal workers

Before, running Temporal workers on Cloud Run services took some workarounds:

  • an HTTP listener, because services expect containers to listen on a port

  • instance-based billing, so workers kept their CPU between requests

  • minimum instances, so the service didn't scale to zero

By running Temporal workers on Cloud Run worker pools, you don’t need those workarounds anymore, and you have:

  • No endpoint to manage. There's no public URL or load balancer to lock down, and no health-check port to implement.

  • Steady CPU at a lower price. Instances don't idle or throttle. Cloud Run doesn't remove instances because they look idle, so Temporal alone decides when the pool shrinks. Worker pools list at almost 40% less per vCPU-hour and GB-hour than instance-billed Cloud Run services.

  • Scaling without revision churn. Changing the instance count doesn't create a new revision, so Temporal can resize the pool as often as the load changes.

How Temporal manages scaling and versioning of worker pools

Temporal decides when to add capacity using one main signal: the delay between a task landing in the task queue backlog and a worker picking it up. If that delay grows, the available workers are saturated. Scaling occurs as follows:

  • Server-side detection: The Temporal server tracks this backlog-to-worker latency for each task queue.

  • Push notification: When the latency crosses its trigger conditions, the server sends a push notification to the worker controller instance.

  • Provisioning: The worker controller then adds capacity to the worker pool. New instances take time to start and connect before they can poll for tasks, so capacity lags behind the signal.

Because Temporal keeps spare capacity, the pool grows ahead of demand instead of after tasks pile up. Scale-in is more conservative. Temporal waits for a stabilization period after the last time a task found no available worker (90 seconds by default), and it pauses between successive reductions. Cloud Run’s configurable graceful shutdown extends shutdown from 10 seconds to 10 minutes. That gives SIGTERM-aware workers time to finish or checkpoint. The instance count stays between a minimum and a maximum that you set. If the first task after an idle period can't wait for an instance to start, set the minimum above zero.

Deploying new workflow code without breaking running executions is hard. Temporal workflows are stateful and deterministic, so if you swap their code mid-run, you get non-determinism errors. Serverless Workers on Cloud Run solve this by requiring Temporal Worker Versioning. You don't patch code with conditional branches. Instead, you deploy each Worker Deployment Version as its own worker pool deployment, identified by a 

deploymentName
and a 
buildId
. Using distinct worker pools solves two problems:

  • Workflows that started on a particular Worker Deployment Version continue to run and complete on that version.

  • Each Worker Deployment Version is scaled and drained individually, matching compute spend and utilization to the requirements of your application. As existing workflows complete and drain on a previous Worker Deployment Version, the underlying Worker Pool is eventually scaled down to zero automatically.

You set a versioning behavior for each Workflow type, or set a Worker-level default:

  • PINNED: A workflow stays on the Worker version (Build ID) it started on and finishes there. Best for short-running workflows, order processing and multi-step APIs.

  • AUTO_UPGRADE: A workflow moves to the new "Current" or "Target" Worker Deployment Version as you roll it out. Best for long-running workflows, such as subscription billing or tasks that run for weeks.

Learn more about configuring worker versioning here.

Get started

Setup takes three steps:

  • Containerize your Temporal Worker and deploy the container as a Cloud Run worker pool, with the Build ID in the pool name. Keep credentials such as your Temporal API key in Secret Manager.

  • Connect Temporal to your worker pool by granting Temporal Cloud permission to manage the worker pool so it can scale it.

  • Create a Worker Deployment Version in Temporal that points at the pool's project, region, and name.

Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run is in preview, so APIs and configuration may change before the stable release. To get started,

  • Learn how Serverless Workers on Cloud Run scale and handle versions.

  • Deploy your first worker with the setup guide.

  • See Cloud Run worker pools for CPU, memory, GPU and networking options.

  • Sign up for the configurable graceful shutdown preview.

entries.content:
Darren Mowry

VP, Global Startups & Investor Ecosystem, Google

Small teams, short runway, and constant pressure to ship faster — it’s the reality we see every day among the founders we work with at Google for Startups. When you are building a company from the ground up, every hour spent on operational overhead or infrastructure plumbing is an hour taken away from your core product.

Last week at Gemini at Work 2026, we introduced the Gemini agent: a single, universal agent designed to work both as your personal assistant and as a dedicated member of your team. And this week, we made our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, widely available — trained to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks.

Here is a look at how the Gemini agent works, five practical takeaways for founders, and how startups are already using it to punch above their weight.

What is the Gemini agent?

Instead of prompting separate chatbots for writing, coding, and data analysis, the Gemini agent is a single agent that takes high-level objectives and returns finished work. Three principles define it:

  • Unified: A single agent can now handle knowledge work, data analysis, creative asset generation, and writing and running code. For complex jobs, it dynamically spins up temporary, job-specific sub-agents and coordinates their work in parallel or in sequence.

  • Omnipresent access: It works across the surfaces you use every day — on the web, command line, desktop, and mobile, as well as natively inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Chat, and Calendar.

  • Persistent: It runs in the cloud with continuous memory across four dimensions (session, semantic, procedural, and episodic). It onboards itself like a new hire — learning your team, tools, and business context so you don't have to re-explain your startup with every prompt, and keeping multi-day tasks moving even after you close your laptop.

For founders wearing five hats at once, Gemini works like a digital chief of staff that's already briefed on your calendar, projects and documents. Ask it to research market trends, build a financial model in Sheets and turn both into a pitch deck, without repeating what the project or goals are at each step. It also works ahead of you. When an investor emails asking for your latest product update as a deck, Gemini spots the request and offers to handle it; one click and it comes back with completed work, ready for sharing or review.

Five takeaways for startups

1. Coworker agents and skills help you scale your output

Beyond personal assistance, you can create persistent coworker agents that work with your entire team. Each agent comes with its own Workspace account, email address, Drive storage, and directory presence. You can define a specific role — such as a launch coordinator, QA triager, or financial analyst — and your teammates can add agents to a Chat space or 

@mention
it in a Google Doc comment to delegate work.

You can also equip agents with reusable skills — or let Gemini write skills for itself as it learns your processes. For example, with operational reporting skills connected to BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog, anyone on your team can ask a plain-language question to build and save a live report. Once saved, those reports run on demand without incurring additional token costs. Gemini also offers pre-built specializations, starting with legal and financial services.

  • What it means for startups: Coworker agents can immediately increase the capacity of your teams, and skills can standardize repeatable processes like investor and operational reporting without burning tokens on every run.

2. Open and third-party model choice

Gemini is the agent, and the model underneath is your choice. As startup architectures mature, sending every task to a single frontier model quickly eats into gross margins. With the Gemini agent, you can dynamically route workloads across Gemini models, third-party models like Anthropic’s Claude, and lightweight open models like Gemma.

  • What it means for startups: You get flexibility without lock-in. You can optimize your cost per task — using compact models for high-volume, deterministic jobs and frontier models for complex reasoning — and swap models as your product evolves without rebuilding your workflows.

3. Connected to your services and tools

An agent is only as useful as the systems it can reach. In addition to Google Workspace, the Gemini agent connects directly to your engineering, data, and business stack, including partner solutions:

  • Development and collaboration: Git, Slack, Jira and more

  • Data and local files: BigQuery, Postgres, Snowflake, Databricks, and more alongside files on your desktop

  • Custom tools via MCP: Any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside your network so your engineers can build and share internal tools.

What it means for startups: Instead of spending engineering cycles maintaining custom connectors, your team can plug the agent straight into your existing codebase, databases, and MCP tools so it can act on live data wherever it lives.

4. Built-in security and governance

For B2B startups, the enterprise security audit is often where deals stall. Under the hood, every agent is assigned a cryptographic Agent Identity for clear audit trails, runs inside an isolated sandbox, and protected with built-in prompt injection defenses. External traffic is routed through Agent Gateway, allowing you to enforce governance policies. And managing coworker agents is as straightforward as managing users today, since they all have a Workspace account.

  • What it means for startups: When an enterprise buyer’s CISO asks how your AI workflows handle data privacy, prompt injection, and access control, you have an enterprise-grade architecture ready — helping you clear procurement hurdles.

5. Protect your runway with real-time cost controls

Autonomous agents that run sub-agents for hours or days can quickly run up a bill if a loop goes unchecked. You can now set hard, real-time spend caps directly in the Cloud Billing Console; if a cap is reached, the project's agent automatically pauses so a bug never turns into a billing surprise. Underneath, Gemini runs on Google’s specialized AI infrastructure, including our inference-optimized TPU 8i, which delivers 80% better performance-per-dollar than the prior generation.

  • What it means for startups: You and your developers can experiment with long-running, parallel agentic loops with a built-in financial safety net that protects your cash reserves and builds confidence with your backers.

Founders already building

Startups and AI-native innovators are already putting Gemini to work. Immersive storytelling platform Whenere used Dreamlands, an agentic 3D worldbuilding platform built on Gemini platform, to bring Pride and Prejudice to Fortnite — with Gemini generating textures for each new object in about 7 seconds for under 10 cents; one artist created nearly 250 custom assets in a single day and completed a historically accurate estate in under a week. They join application-building platform Lovable and fellow startups and innovators including  OpenEvidence, Recursion, and Replit and more.

Build with Google for Startups

The agentic era gives lean teams the leverage to punch far above their weight — whether you’re deploying coworker agents to cover internal operations or building agentic workflows directly into your product.

While these new Gemini agent capabilities are not publicly available yet, startups can contact our sales team to learn more and discuss how to get ready. In the meantime, you can explore the Google for Startups program to access credits, hands-on technical guidance, mentorship, global founder community programs and more.

entries.content:
Pratik Bhangale

Product Manager, Google Cloud

Agents represent a fundamental shift in cloud operations. They can act on behalf of users or autonomously, make non-deterministic decisions, and request data across projects at unprecedented speed and scale. Because agents are a distinct category of non-human identity (NHI), they require unique secure-by-default guardrails.

Traditional, manually-operated network perimeters are vulnerable to today’s machine-speed attacks. Overly permissive perimeters, built to avoid blocked connections, increase the risk of unauthorized data theft, but overly strict perimeters stall development under a flood of access denials.

Today, we're excited to announce key enhancements to VPC Service Controls (VPC-SC) that make perimeters easier to create, maintain, and scale. You can now add folders to perimeter membership, so that projects contained in them inherit policy. You can also manage granular exceptions and resolve denials with guided, scoped remediation. 

The result is data protected by default, so you can scale autonomous agents across your enterprise without letting data leave your perimeter. This update is generally available, and at no additional cost.

Perimeters aligned to your architecture

VPC-SC provides a context-aware network security perimeter around your Google Cloud deployment, designed to secure your organization against data theft, even in the event of compromised credentials, identity and access management (IAM) misconfigurations, and insider threats. By extending network-layer protection across service-to-service interactions in Google Cloud's infrastructure, VPC-SC goes beyond traditional firewalls and creates an additional layer of defense that prevents access outside your corporate network — and is now easier for your organization to manage.

Cloud administrators configuring VPC-SC can now include folders in perimeter membership, automatically extending the folder’s access policy to every project and nested subfolder it contains. New workloads can inherit protection by default, with no further modification.

Figure 1: Simplified perimeter authoring in VPC-SC.

Perimeter membership updates when a project is moved, simplifying lifecycle maintenance. Security coverage follows the resource hierarchy that your organization already governs, and compliance verification requires only confirming that the resource is located in the correct part of the hierarchy.

Dry-run mode also supports folder membership, helping administrators evaluate the effect of a hierarchy-wide perimeter against live traffic before enforcement.

Folder and organization support in ingress and egress rules

Well-defined ingress and egress rules establish granular, context-aware perimeters without sacrificing operational flexibility across complex multi-project environments. Security administrators can now specify Google Cloud folders and organizations directly within those rules. A single hierarchy reference stands in for the set of projects beneath it, which keeps rules concise, keeps attribute counts well within quota limits, and extends access automatically to projects created later in the hierarchy.

Figure 2 : Simplified authoring of ingress/egress rules.

Using Private Service Connect endpoints in ingress and egress rules

Enterprises increasingly use private paths to reach desired endpoints in their deployment instead of exposing the traffic to the internet. Private Service Connect endpoints for Google APIs are now supported as an attribute in ingress and egress rules. Administrators can author a rule that authorizes access specifically over a designated private endpoint, producing a policy that corresponds directly to the connectivity architecture it is intended to govern.

Figure 3: Supporting Private Service Connect endpoints with ingress and egress rules.

For organizations that have standardized on Private Service Connect, including endpoints propagated across the estate through Network Connectivity Center, this provides both a more precise and a more concise means of expressing source for the request.

Service patterns in VPC accessible services

Service patterns in VPC accessible services provide granular control over Google APIs accessed with private Virtual IP addresses (VIP), permitting interoperability beyond just VPC-SC integrated services. If the workload requires controlled access to validated API endpoints over a private path, administrators can now allow only the specific API URL patterns required. 

Additionally, the capability supports appending org-restriction-headers with egress requests to facilitate access to only authorized domains and resources. Because you don’t need to manage egress-proxy, you can accommodate legitimate operational requirements while maintaining a tightly-bounded private path, instead of choosing between a broad allowance and no access at all.

Figure 4: Granular control over Google APIs with service patterns in VPC accessible services.

Guided violation remediation

VPC-SC perimeter policies evolve continuously alongside the workloads they protect, and administrators periodically need to authorize a legitimate access request not yet covered. New Guided Violation Remediation in VPC-SC Violation Analyzer cuts resolution time for blocked requests from days to minutes by generating a policy fix with remediation recommendations, which you can validate in Dry-Run mode first. 

Rather than just diagnosing why the violation occurred for a given denial, Violation Analyzer evaluates the blocked request against the applicable perimeter configuration, and proposes a specific configuration change, narrowly scoped by least-privilege design principles, to authorize the traffic: an ingress rule, an egress rule, an access level, or an update to VPC accessible services. This relieves pressure on administrators to broadly open up a perimeter just to resolve a violation and get an application working quickly.

Read more about how BlackLine uses Violation Analyzer to streamline investigations.

Figure 5 : VPC-SC Violation Remediation for faster turn-around.

Get started today

VPC-SC makes it simple and automated to deploy and refine granular network perimeter protection, even for autonomous agents. To get started:

  • Establish your folder baseline: Identify the folders in your resource hierarchy that correspond to the boundaries you intend to enforce, and define perimeters around them so that new workloads inherit policy on creation.

  • Run risk-free in Dry-Run mode: Observe production traffic safely without blocking active developers.

  • Unblock traffic with Violation Analyzer and Violation Dashboard: Use automated least-privilege remediation recommendations to resolve any denials that surface.

  • Enforce with confidence: Secure your full data estate by transitioning to enforcement once your dry-run logs show your intended access with clean, authorized traffic.

To learn more about how VPC-SC can help simplify your data security posture and confidently secure your autonomous agent fleets, check out the VPC-SC documentation.

Welcome to the first Cloud CISO Perspectives for October 2026. Today, Stephanie Kiel explains the latest on our approach to post-quantum cryptography, and shares a new tool to help CISOs and executives prepare their organizations for PQC.

As with all Cloud CISO Perspectives, the contents of this newsletter are posted to the Google Cloud blog. If you’re reading this on the website and you’d like to receive the email version, you can subscribe here.

New Gemini Notebook can help CISOs and policymakers prepare for PQC

By Stephanie Kiel, Head of Cloud Security Policy, Government Affairs and Public Policy, Google Cloud

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is one of the most urgent security shifts of the decade — and one of the easiest to tune out. For security leaders and policymakers, the research is dense, scattered across papers and engineering blogs, and can be challenging to turn into action.

To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography, a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place. Ask it questions, listen to an audio overview, or test yourself with flashcards, and quickly get up to speed on the quantum threat.

Why PQC matters now

Quantum computing is rapidly moving from theory to reality. Our Willow chip and Quantum Echoes algorithm mark substantial progress, and Google research estimates that breaking ECDLP-256 and RSA-2048 encryption — the public-key cryptography schemes protecting much of our online data — would require around 500,000 and 1 million imperfect quantum computer components (noisy qubits), respectively.

To help, we're launching Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography, a public Gemini Notebook that brings Google's PQC research, engineering blogs, and migration guidance together in one place.

This research has consequences now. It indicates that today’s online security is more vulnerable to future quantum computers than previously thought.

In Store Now, Decrypt Later attacks, adversaries may steal encrypted data now and wait to decrypt it once a sufficiently powerful quantum computer exists. Data that we’ve long considered sensitive — health records, financial data, intellectual property, and government secrets — is already at risk. 

With continued advances in architecture, quantum algorithms, and quantum error correction shrinking future quantum hardware requirements, waiting to upgrade our digital locks is not a viable option. To help organizations stay ahead of the curve, Google has published a migration timeline noting our plans to transition to PQC by 2029, and we urge others to consider the same.

As the technology advances, policymakers should consider urging critical infrastructure owners and operators to recognize condensed timelines, and build PQC readiness into existing risk mitigation plans. We also recommend governments engage with global counterparts to promote a harmonized approach to standards development, and include technical and security experts in the building of policy and regulatory requirements focused on quantum safety.

Google's PQC expertise, in one notebook

The Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography notebook turns years of Google expertise into an interactive primer that anyone can use. It's built on curated Google sources covering the quantum era, quantum computing breakthroughs like Willow, Quantum Echoes, and surface code error suppression, industry PQC standards, Google's own deployments, and the latest research.

In the Gemini Notebook, you can:

  • Get answers grounded in Google's sources.

  • Listen to a podcast-style audio overview.

  • Test your PQC knowledge with flashcards.

  • Explore an interactive visual diagram of the quantum threat.

  • Read a concise briefing document.

Try these prompts

To get started, here are a few questions to ask the notebook:

  • For CISOs: "What should a CISO prioritize in the first 90 days of a PQC migration?"

  • For anyone new to PQC: "Explain store-now-decrypt-later in plain terms."

  • For developers: "How does hybrid ML-KEM key exchange work in Chrome?"

As with all generative AI, the notebook can make mistakes, so check its responses against the linked sources.

What's at stake

Previous cryptographic migrations, such as moving from SHA-1 or upgrading TLS, have taken a decade or more. Waiting for the availability of a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer before beginning the migration journey represents a significant security risk given the importance of public-key cryptography for securing digital essentials like web traffic, software updates, digital identities, and signatures.

For CISOs, we recommend that you start by:

  • Understanding where vulnerable cryptography lives in your organization.

  • Identifying and prioritizing data and systems most at risk from quantum threats, and developing a plan for addressing these risks.

  • Anticipate system-wide effects that PQC migration could have.

  • Building crypto-agility into your security plans, using learnings from past experiences like Heartbleed.

Additional detail on these recommendations is available in our previous blog post.  

For the broader security community, the transition only succeeds if this knowledge is accessible to everyone — not just organizations with dedicated cryptography teams.

How Google is putting PQC into practice

We’ve been deploying PQC for years. Highlights include:

  • Hybrid Kyber/ML-KEM key exchange protecting Chrome traffic

  • PQC in Android

  • Quantum-safe digital signatures in Cloud KMS

  • PQC for Google's internal communications

  • Wiz PQC readiness scanner across code, cloud, and runtime

We also co-founded the Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance at the Linux Foundation with industry leaders including Amazon Web Services, Cisco, IBM, and NVIDIA to support open-source tools like Open Quantum Safe.

Build a PQC notebook for your own team

Here’s how you can create a resource similar to our PQC Gemini Notebook, specific to your organization’s needs:

  • Curate trusted sources. Start with a focused set of authoritative research, standards, and guidance.

  • Write neutral prompts. Keep instructions factual so outputs stay grounded in your sources.

  • Add AI disclaimers and a welcome note. Tell readers what the notebook covers and remind them that AI can make mistakes.

  • Review all output with human oversight. Have experts check every artifact before you share it.

Start preparing today

The quantum transition has already started, but preparing your organization doesn't have to begin with a 100-page whitepaper. Start by understanding the threat, then assess your cryptographic inventory and build a migration roadmap.

You can get started with the Prepare for Post-Quantum Cryptography Gemini Notebook and share it with your team today. To learn more about Google Cloud’s approach to PQC, check out our dedicated Google Cloud PQC Resource Hub.

In case you missed it

Here are the latest updates, products, services, and resources from our security teams so far this month:

  • The Wiz Red Agent caught a Fortune 500 firm’s data exposure that other tools missed: Using an attacker’s mindset, the Red Agent found a public page exposing sensitive data in minutes. Read more.
  • Chrome's response to recent ccTLD registry hijacks: Following recent .gh, .sl, and .as ccTLD domain hijacks, Chrome immediately blocked unauthorized HTTPS certificates via CRLSets to protect users automatically. Read more.

  • Introducing Wiz AI SAST: Application security that understands you: Find, validate, and fix complex business logic flaws with an AI code scanner backed by Wiz Research, operationalized in your existing security program. Read more.
  • Introducing WizOS Helm Charts to secure the Kubernetes supply chain: WizOS Helm Charts can help eliminate hidden CI/CD risks and unmaintained dependencies with hardened, signed, and CVE-scanned charts for Kubernetes. Read more.
  • What’s new in Wiz Service Catalog: Smarter discovery, governance, and service-level context can help build your service catalog faster, keep service context current, and give teams a clearer path from cloud risk to accountability. Read more.

Threat Intelligence news

Here’s our containment and remediation guidance. Read more.

entries.title: Predictable AI spend in BigQuery: Introducing cost management for generative AI functions
entries.summary: The generative AI functions in BigQuery (AI.GENERATE, AI.IF, AI.CLASSIFY, AI.SCORE, and more) bring large language models (LLMs) directly into your SQL, so a single query can classify millions of support tickets or score each product review for sentiment. However, because these functions are billed by the token, scaling them across massive datasets highlights the importance of managing your budget
entries.content:
Tushar Jaiswal

Software Engineer

Alicia Williams

Developer Advocate

The generative AI functions in BigQuery (

AI.GENERATE
, 
AI.IF
, 
AI.CLASSIFY
, 
AI.SCORE
, and more) bring large language models (LLMs) directly into your SQL, so a single query can classify millions of support tickets or score each product review for sentiment. However, because these functions are billed by the token, scaling them across massive datasets highlights the importance of managing your budget proactively. 

We recently announced the general availability (GA) of token-based cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions: daily quotas that let administrators set self-serve guardrails on AI token consumption, so teams can innovate while staying within your budget. In this blog, we provide an overview of cost management for BigQuery generative AI functions, walk through a few practical examples, and share resources to help you get started. Let’s jump in.  

Quotas for managing costs

Four daily quotas, managed through the Google Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM) quota system, provide controls at the project level and the per-user level. Per-user limits apply to each user within a project, not across your organization.

Key details:

  • The quotas are global. Usage is summed across all regions, so costs can't pile up unnoticed in a region you weren't watching.

  • Output quotas include "thinking" tokens. Reasoning tokens count toward your output quota, just as they count toward your Gemini platform bill.

Which functions are covered?

The quotas apply to these BigQuery functions that perform LLM-backed generation:

  • AI.GENERATE

  • AI.GENERATE_TABLE

  • AI.GENERATE_TEXT
    (and its alias 
    ML.GENERATE_TEXT
    )

  • AI.CLASSIFY

  • AI.IF

  • AI.SCORE

  • AI.AGG

What's not covered: Embedding functions such as 

AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING
(also available as 
ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING
) and 
AI.EMBED
 are not subject to these quotas, because they run on different, substantially cheaper models.

Managing your quotas

Administrators can view and adjust the quotas directly in the Google Cloud console as workloads change, with no support case required.

  • Navigate to IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

  • Filter by service and select BigQuery API.

  • Sort by the Name column to bring the four AI quotas to the top.

Locating the gen AI token quotas in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

4. Find the quota, for example AI input tokens per day.

5. Open the three-dot menu and choose Edit quota.

From there:

  • To tighten cost control, lower a quota. This takes effect immediately with no approval needed.

  • To support higher usage, request an increase from the same page. Many requests are auto-approved; larger increases may go through a quick review.

Editing a gen AI token quota in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

You'll need the right permissions. You need one of: Owner, Editor, Quota Administrator (

roles/servicemanagement.quotaAdmin
), or Service Usage Admin (
roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin
).

Prefer automation? You can also manage these quotas programmatically through the Cloud Quotas API, the 

gcloud
CLI, and Terraform to apply consistent guardrails across projects.

Monitoring usage

Beyond setting limits, the Quotas & System Limits page displays your historical token consumption so you can quickly detect spikes and right-size your budgets. Use these trends to see how new generative AI workloads and data pipelines affect your overall token usage.

Daily project-level token usage for a gen AI token quota in IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits.

Longer-term usage graph with selectable 7-day, 14-day, 30-day, and custom ranges.

For a step-by-step walkthrough, see the BigQuery documentation on controlling costs with token quotas.

Token quotas vs. billing spend caps

Token quotas aren't the only cost guardrail in Google Cloud.

  • Token quotas (this feature) are preventive and AI-specific. BigQuery tracks token usage during query execution and stops work close to the limit, with separate limits per project and per user.

  • Cloud Billing spend caps operate on dollars at the project and service level and can automatically block usage when a threshold is reached. They're a broad, financial backstop rather than a precise usage control, and because enforcement is not instant, some overages are incurred.

Use token quotas as your first line of defense for AI spend, and a spend cap as a project-wide safety net.

How enforcement works

Quotas are enforced by stopping work rather than letting a query run past your limit. A query is rejected up front with a 

QuotaExceeded
error only if a quota it needs is already exhausted. Otherwise, it starts, and if a quota runs out mid-query, BigQuery stops sending new LLM calls:

  • Functions that support 

    max_error_ratio
    (such as 
    AI.IF
    ) return partial results if unprocessed rows stay within the ratio, and otherwise fail.

  • General-purpose functions (such as 

    AI.GENERATE
    ) still succeed. Skipped rows have no generated value, and their 
    status
    field contains the quota-exceeded error.

For details, see quota enforcement behavior in the documentation.

Sizing your input data: 
AI.COUNT_TOKENS

To choose quota values, it helps to know how much text your workloads send to a model. The 

AI.COUNT_TOKENS
function helps with this.

AI.COUNT_TOKENS
returns the number of tokens a model's tokenizer produces for a text string, without making a billable generation call. Run it over a column to measure your input data:

The count is a lower bound on input tokens. It doesn't include output or thinking tokens, the instructions each AI function adds around your input, or non-text inputs such as images. Use it to:

  • Gauge the input side of a workload before you launch it.

  • Right-size your quotas together with a small sample run that measures actual input and output usage.

  • Translate tokens into dollars using the published Gemini platform pricing for your model.

From tokens to budget: a worked example

Suppose you want to keep a project's daily AI spend around $100 with the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite model. As of today's published pricing (BigQuery processes in batch which provides a 50% discount):

  • Input tokens: $0.125 per 1 million tokens

  • Output tokens (response + reasoning): $0.75 per 1 million tokens

If a small sample run shows an average 100:1 input-to-output token ratio, you can solve for a daily budget:

Solving gives about 754 million input tokens and 7.54 million output tokens per day. Set AI input tokens per day and AI output tokens per day to these values to hold the project near $100/day. If a project uses models with different prices, budget per model or blend the rates.

Best practices for managing AI cost

  • Start with per-user quotas. They stop one user or runaway experiment from draining the project's budget.

  • Measure before you scale. Use 

    AI.COUNT_TOKENS
    to size your input, then check a small sample run in the usage chart before setting limits.

  • Mind the output side. Output tokens cost more. Where a function accepts 

    max_output_tokens
    , set it to bound generation length.

  • Monitor and iterate. Adjust limits as real usage and budgets change.

Get started

Token-based cost management is available now. To begin:

  • Open IAM & Admin → Quotas & System Limits in the Google Cloud Console and filter by BigQuery API.

  • Review the four AI-related token quotas and set limits that match your budget.

  • Use 

    AI.COUNT_TOKENS
    to size your input data.

For the full details, see the documentation on controlling generative AI costs.

With token-based guardrails in place, your teams can use generative AI in BigQuery with the cost predictability your organization needs.

entries.content:
Praveen Kumar

Customer Engineer, Data & AI

The reality for most organizations is that data lives everywhere. As engineering teams expand and adopt specialized platforms for their workloads, enterprise data naturally disperses across multiple clouds and operational systems. When analytical and AI initiatives require context from across the entire organization,these teams traditionally face a difficult trade-off: build complex extraction pipelines to copy data into a central repository or accept fragmented reporting.

Traditional architectures address this fragmentation with scheduled extraction pipelines that copy remote datasets into a central staging warehouse. This approach creates synchronization lag, adds recurring storage costs, and triggers variable network egress fees. When schemas change upstream, pipelines break, and teams spend hours reconciling metrics across out-of-sync dashboards.

BigQuery and Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse offer a streamlined way to solve this challenge with a foundation based on the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification. Rather than moving data to the compute engine, you can bring Google Cloud compute and generative AI directly to your data, querying it in place across Databricks, Snowflake, and AWS Glue.

In this post, we walk through how to configure Databricks Unity Catalog for federation into BigQuery (AWS Glue and Snowflake set up in appendix), run a single query joining data across all three external catalogs, and use conversational analytics in BigQuery to explore the consolidated data with natural language.

Figure 1: BigQuery federates metadata across external Apache Iceberg REST catalogs through Lakehouse, enabling in-place conversational analytics without data migration.

The borderless lakehouse architecture

This solution uses Lakehouse runtime catalog to synchronize metadata from other cloud providers, allowing you to query data with BigQuery or external open source engines through the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, all without migrating the data. Because Databricks Unity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon Catalog, and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the open Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification, you can apply a consistent connection pattern across all three platforms.

When you run a federated query, Lakehouse runtime catalog separates metadata synchronization from storage access:

  • Metadata synchronization: Lakehouse runtime catalog periodically syncs schemas, snapshot pointers, and table definitions from the remote catalog based on a refresh schedule you define.

  • Direct storage access: During query runtime, a compatible engine reads Parquet data files directly from remote object storage, such as Amazon S3, using temporary credentials issued by the remote platform.

All query processing runs within Google cloud compute such as BigQuery or Managed Service  for Apache Spark. Remote Databricks clusters, Snowflake virtual warehouses, and AWS compute instances are not invoked during execution.

Authentication follows an explicit three-step deployment pattern: create the federated catalog in Google Cloud, inspect its configuration to retrieve its automatically generated service account, and grant access permissions within the remote platform.

You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided below.

Configure Databricks Unity Catalog

We begin in Databricks by preparing the catalog and table. In Unity Catalog, federated access requires that your target schema be associated with an external location registered in Databricks:

  • You can use AI to generate sample data. The schema details for tables are provided in each section.

Before external engines can read this table, a Databricks metastore administrator must enable External data access on the metastore details tab.

Go to Databricks Admin account and under User Management, create a Databricks Service Principal and make a note of its UUID 

"6ea7b861-c5a5-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"

Connect Databricks to BigQuery

Next, create the federated catalog inside Google Cloud using the 

gcloud
command-line tool. You will need your Databricks workspace URL and the application ID of your Databricks service principal:

Once created, describe the catalog to view its assigned service account:

Return to Databricks to assign permissions to your service principal:

You must grant the 

EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA
privilege to the Databricks Service Principal on the target schemas or catalog to enable credential vending for external data access.

Finally, to complete the connection, configure the federation policy on the Databricks service principal with the following details -

  • Issuer URL* -  https://accounts.google.com

entries.title: Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud, built to help solve your business’ hardest problems
entries.summary: Last week we announced that Gemini Enterprise has evolved to make it even simpler to get work done, and introduced the Gemini agent, your new universal agent for work. It's always on and ready to answer your questions. It will write code, complete longer and more complex tasks, or perform whatever you need to get the job done, all from a single prompt box. And model intelligence underpins it all.
entries.content:
Michael Gerstenhaber

VP, Product Management, Gemini, Google Cloud

Last week we announced that Gemini Enterprise has evolved to make it even simpler to get work done, and introduced the Gemini agent, your new universal agent for work. It's always on and ready to answer your questions. It will write code, complete longer and more complex tasks, or perform whatever you need to get the job done, all from a single prompt box. And model intelligence underpins it all.

To enable a new frontier of work, we are making our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, available on Google Cloud. 

We trained Argon to work with both depth and precision, which allows it to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks which are reinforced with strong domain expertise along the way. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like CodeMender, Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish. 

Customers and partners using Gemini 4 Argon

Four ways Argon changes how your business works

1. Hand off your hardest work

Your teams already use Gemini for business to answer questions and draft content. With Argon, they can hand off the deep, multi-step work that used to take hours or days, and get back finished work they can use.

Argon reads long documents that mix text, tables, charts and images, and turns them into one clear output grounded in those sources. It can pull findings from many sources into a single structured answer, analyze data over time, and write stronger legal, finance, and executive documents. On long tasks, it keeps going until the job is done. We trained Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause for confirmation before taking irreversible steps, and it tells you when it couldn't find something or finish a task.

Customers who tested Argon tell us it excels at turning huge, unstructured inputs into cohesive outputs.

"As software development becomes more agentic, teams need models that can support long-running, multi-step work across all stages of the development lifecycle. Gemini 4 Argon is designed to help organizations bring AI into development, security, and operations while keeping it within established enterprise workflows and controls.” – Stuart Moncada, VP, GitLab.

2. Precise, verifiable results on the work that drives your business

In finance, legal, tax, and other regulated work, calculations and data extraction need to be precise, repeatable, and verifiable.

For financial quantitative work, Argon can help automate multi-step ledger reconciliations, spreadsheet formulas, and variance analyses. It delivers high calculation integrity, citation fidelity, and formula accuracy across quantitative models. The proof is in the numbers: Argon leads on the Vals Index, which measures economic impact across finance, coding, legal, and tax work.

In legal research, Argon can help legal teams review case law and regulatory filings to pull out verified citations and key precedents. It leads on domain-specific evaluations like Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark for legal research and drafting, with strong citation fidelity and direct answers when helping teams evaluate complex legal precedents.

"Gemini 4 Argon shows how much progress Google has made on agentic legal reasoning. We saw substantial improvements over Gemini 3.1 Pro across our legal agent evaluations, particularly in corporate M&A, data privacy and cybersecurity, and EC/VC. Accuracy also held up on long-document analysis, an encouraging result for lawyers working through detailed transactional matters." – Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research, Harvey.

“We collaborated with Google on NowAI-Bench to help shape Gemini 4 for key enterprise work. In early access, it delivered roughly 20% improved task success than Gemini 3.8 Flash, with standout gains in HR and customer service. On the ServiceNow AI Platform, our L1 Service Desk AI specialist brings Google’s most advanced intelligence, governed and secure, turning tasks into fully autonomous work.” - Nenshad Bardoliwalla, Senior Vice President, AI Products, ServiceNow.

3. Build and ship products faster

Argon is built to handle complex, multi-step projects from start to finish. Our customers consistently ask for intelligence that can break down goals, track progress, and update multiple files at the same time.

"Gemini 4 Argon handles complex tasks reliably, from 3D games to rich animations. In Figma Make, it helps teams turn their most ambitious, multi-step ideas into impressive prototypes.” – Loredana Crisan, Chief Design Officer, Figma.

To see how well Argon handles this, we put it to work on our own tools. The team behind our open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK) set out to reduce framework overhead and improve code performance while maintaining full compatibility with existing applications. Working autonomously overnight within automated testing guardrails, Argon surfaced optimizations, now live in google/adk-python, that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and speed up cold imports by 21%. To learn more, read the engineering deep dive here.

Across Google, engineering teams using Argon in Google Antigravity have increased agentic code submissions by more than 35% while cutting code rollbacks by nearly a third. The Chrome team used Argon to finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files in Chromium's 40 million-line codebase, completing months of work in weeks. Argon's improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision and visual coding also make it faster to go from idea to working prototype.

For more advanced algorithms, our code optimization and discovery agent AlphaEvolve uses Argon to deliver strong performance improvements across real-world enterprise workloads, including factory scheduling, logistics, game code speed-ups, and chip layout — as well as complex mathematical benchmarks, and more. 

To learn how to best use Argon, check out the developer's guide.

4. Stronger defense for your code and business

While Argon has cyber mitigations that block offensive tasks such as pentesting and exploitation, you can still take full advantage of Argon’s defensive capabilities using CodeMender to find and fix vulnerabilities, or use Argon with your own security harness. It ties for first place on CWE-Bench v1 with a top score of 68% for remediating security vulnerabilities.

"We are integrating Gemini 4 Argon into MarketingX for automated codebase security audits. In our evaluations, the model successfully identified 100% of top-priority vulnerabilities with 0% fabricated vulnerabilities across verified claims. This precision unlocks proactive, code-level security for our customers before deployment.” - Yunus Emre, Chief AI Officer of AI Lab, HubX.

Security also means being able to trust Argon inside your own environment. Argon is our most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections, where malicious instructions or context are used to hijack a model’s behavior. It leads the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, cutting attack success across 15 adaptive attempts to 0.7%. That matters when Argon reads email, documents and webpages that may contain hidden malicious instructions.

We are also releasing Argon without cyber guardrails to a select set of trusted defenders, which allows for testing a full breadth of cybersecurity capabilities. Trusted defenders are vetted through our Fairwind Program, a limited access initiative that provides government, critical infrastructure, and cybersecurity partners exclusive, unmitigated access to advanced  models. 

Enterprise customers and partners in our early access program are already seeing strong wins with Argon.

Leaders from Amplitude, Deloitte, and Rakuten share Gemini 4 Argon results

Get started

Starting today, Gemini 4 Argon is available in Gemini for business on the web, desktop, and mobile. Enterprise developers and builders can access Argon via API in Gemini platform under model ID 

gemini-4-argon
, in Google AI Studio, and in Google Antigravity.

Argon launches at an introductory rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off. After November 30, standard pricing of $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens will apply. Review the model card and developer guide for complete technical specifications, token limits, and migration instructions.

Cyber defenders can join us at Security Summit to learn how to use Gemini 4 Argon to defend against machine-speed threats and automate remediation.
